content_metadata.description: A scientific demonstration showcasing the combustion reaction of a gummy bear with potassium chlorate, led by Dr. Tricia Scott, with student interactions for explanations and questions.

activities.description: Dr. Scott introduces the experiment, "Death of a Gummy Bear" Combustion Demo.
Dr. Scott explains the first step, melting potassium chlorate.
Dr. Scott pulls down the fume hood sash and starts heating the potassium chlorate.
Dr. Scott explains that after the potassium chlorate melts, they will add the gummy bear.
Dr. Scott discusses the concept of activation energy, explaining that the higher temperature will provide the reacting molecules with enough energy to overcome the activation energy barrier.
Dr. Scott continues to heat the potassium chlorate, waiting for it to melt completely.

characterInteraction.description: Dr. Scott addresses the audience directly, explaining the experiment and the underlying scientific concepts.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Dr. Scott emphasizes the importance of safety precautions by conducting the experiment inside a fume hood.

activities.description: Dr. Scott turns off the lights to make the reaction more visible.
Dr. Scott drops the gummy bear into the molten potassium chlorate.
A vigorous combustion reaction starts, producing bright purple flames and smoke.
Dr. Scott points out the importance of conducting the experiment inside the fume hood due to the intensity of the reaction.

characterInteraction.description: Dr. Scott interacts with the reaction, observing it closely and commenting on its intensity.

scenes.contextualRelevance: The dramatic visual of the combustion reaction serves as a powerful reminder of the energy stored in seemingly harmless substances.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Dr. Scott emphasizes the need for safety precautions.

activities.description: Dr. Scott turns the lights back on.
Dr. Scott asks the students if anyone noticed the color of the flame.
Dr. Scott explains that the purple color is not due to the gummy bear but to the potassium in the potassium chlorate, referencing its characteristic lavender flame color.
She asks if anyone has any questions.
